In the Mail
and Empire's report of the nomination proceedings for the Local Legislature which took place yesterday in the county of Peel, Mr. Fallis, a gentleman whose name the House is familiar with in connection with

certain horse deals in that county, and who is a candidate for re-election, is reported as having said:
That following the investigation he had met Mr. Thompson, K.C., who had conducted the investigation for the Government, and Mr. Thompson had assured him that the investigation had been a full and frank one, and that there was no possibility of legal action against Mr. Fallis. All that any person could say was that as a member he was injudicious in having anything to do with the matter.
I know Mr. Thompson personally, and have a very high regard for him; and, knowing him as I do, I cannot believe that he would give any such statement in advance of the commissioner's opinion. I think the House and the country have a right to know whether he is correctly reported, and I would therefore ask the minister who has to do with this matter to make inquiries, so as to be able to advise us whether or not Mr. Thompson made such a statement.

If the hon. gentleman is referring to me, I do not know that I have any right to ask Mr. Thompson any such a question. Mr. Thompson is a private practising lawyer, and has just as much right to express his opinions as the hon. member for Pictou has. He is a free lawyer, just the same as my hon. friend.

The minister cannot disown Mr. Thompson; or, if he can, the Minister of Justice cannot. Mr. Thompson was the public official who was employed for the purpose of conducting the investigations before the Davidson Commission. He and I are not in the same position at all. I am here as a representative of the people, and have a right to ask this question. Mr. Thompson was the servant of the people and of the Government, and the Government have a right to inquire whether he prejudged the case.

Mr. Thompson has been doing the legal work in connection with the inquiry, and doing it gratuitously. While he is not " employed," strictly speaking, I should imagine he is at perfect liberty to express his views. It is not part of my business to go running around after newspaper reports; when that report comes to this House, we shall be able to deal with it.

I should like to know what the Minister of Justice has to say as to the irresponsibility of Mr. Thompson in prejudging this matter. I suppose the Minister of Justice has something to do with this matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. O. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I have not had the advantage of hearing what the matter was about, I cannot very well say anything in regard to it. I may say, however, that Mr. Thompson was selected by the commissioner to aid him in carrying on his investigation. I may say that that investigation is carried on by the commissioner upon his responsibility to the public of Canada, and that the Minister of Justice would consider he was going very far out of his way if he tried in any manner to interfere with the v ork of the commissioner, who is charged to carry on an absolutely impartial investigation.

He was appointed
upon your recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The commission was appointed upon my recommendation, and I have no reason to be otherwise than proud of that recommendation; furthermore, I am satisfied that the public of Canada, both now and after the report is made, will join with me in the opinion that no better man could have been chosen to make that investigation than Sir Charles Davidson.

I was not speaking about Sir Charles Davidson at all. The Minister of Justice cannot disclaim responsibility for the counsel who was appointed to represent the people in this investigation. If the high ideals which my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce very properly placed before the Canadian people last night are to be denied by his colleagues within twenty-four hours, it is just as well for us to know. I want to tell the Minister of Justice that as a lawyer he cannot tell me or any other lawyer in this country that, as the advisor of the Crown who recommended the appointment of this commission, he has nothing whatever to do with Mr. Thompson, the counsel, who, according to the Mail and Empire's report, has prejudged this case, by saying what could or could not be done with Mr. Fallis.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have pointed out how Mr. Thompson came to be the counsel to the commission. I have no desire to say anything else than that I thoroughly agree in the opinion which the commissioner evidently entertained of Mr. Thompson when he retained him as counsel.
I am not blaming Mr. Thompson at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Who is the hon. gentleman blaming?

My bon. friend did not wait to hear what I was going to say.
I say I know Mr. Thompson very well, and believe him to be a gentleman of rectitude. According to the Mail and Empire* the statement was made yesterday by Mr. Fallis, at the nomination proceedings in the county of Peel, that after the investigation, Mr. Thompson had assured him that the investigation had been full and frank; that there was no possibility of any legal action against Mr. Fallis, and that all that any person could say was that perhaps as a member he was injudicious in having anything to do with the matter. From what I know of Mr. Thompson I have every confidence in him, and I cannot believe that he prejudged the case. He would certainly be considered as having been lax in his duties if he did so. If possible, I want to. find out if my bon. friend can ascertain if it is true that Mr. Thompson did prejudge the case -as Mr. Fallis said he did.

The Minister of Militia said so.

Having appointed a man of high reputation, wide experience and unimpeachable character, an appointment commended by the press and by public opinion throughout the country, we felt that we had adequately discharged a public duty in selecting a man of that type for the inquiry which he was commissioned to make. His -report is not yet before the House. When it comes before the House, hon. members may make- any criticism they see fit of the conduct of the commission or of its finding; but in the meam time I do not think its proceedings ought to be commented upon or d-isou-ssed in this House.
On the Orders of the Day:

In regard to
the Shell Committee, perhaps we shall have the papers promised the other day by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

Apparently

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Neither the Board of

Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 33, to amend the Bank Act. He said:
The principle of this legislation was dis-

cussed at some length on the occasion of the consideration in Committee of the Whole of the resolution preceding the Bill. For the information of the House, and as showing the point of view of myself, of the bankers, and of the farmers of the West, I propose to place on Hansard certain correspondence. First, I shall give a letter which I addressed to the banks, and then some extracts from the replies received from the banks. I shall also place upon Hansard a copy of the resolution which was telegraphed to me on behalf of the United Farmers of Alberta. The letter which I wrote is as follows:
Ottawa, December 24, 1915.
Dear Sir,-For some time past I have had under consideration the question of an amendment to the Bank Act authorizing the banks to take as security for advances to farmers liens upon cattle and certain other live stock. It would seem that such liens should be registered in order that the rights of other creditors might not be prejudiced. The question as you know is one which has been much canvassed at successive revisions of the Bank Act and there has been a conflict of view as to the expediency of such legislation. As it is greatly desirable at this juncture of our affairs that production should be facilitated in every way possible I should appreciate an early expression of your views upon the following questions:
1.	Would such legislation facilitate and lead to increased advances by your bank to the stock-raising community and would it tend to increase production?
2.	Will there be during the coming year sufficient bank credits available for all the increased production possible to the Canadian agricultural and stock-raising community?
3.	If the answer to (2) is in the negative, can you suggest any feasible plan for increasing the available banking credits for the purpose in view?
As I am exceedingly interested in the matter referred to I shall be greatly obliged for a full and frank expression of your views.
Yours very truly,
W. T. White, Minister of Finance.
I propose, if the House will permit me, to read extracts, first, from letters received from banks favourable to this legislation, and then extracts from letters of those believing that this measure will not aceom-plish the object I have in view. First, I give the letters favourable to the legislation :	.
Referring to your letter No. 1904-15 we certainly think the answer to the question asked by the Minister of Finance should be in the affirmative. The development of the live stock industry in the Western States has been greatly accelerated by bank loans rendered possible only by the fact that the banks there have power to take chattel mortgage security on the stock.
It seems likely that in making advances to farmers, banks will continue to be guided principally by consideration of the prospective borrower's character, his demonstrated ability as a farmer, and the financial position shown by his statement, but, as in the case of recent legislation authorizing loans against the pledge of threshed grain, there will be a percentage of cases where the pledge will turn the scale and therefore, in the opinion of this bank, the proposed legislation would be helpful and have a tendency to increase production.
Our Western supervisor is of the opinion that if the banks could legally take security from farmers on live stock it would greatly tend to increase production. He states that there are many farmers in Western Canada whose financial responsibility does not warrant unsecured advances, but whose honesty entitles them to assistance from the bank if we could get unassailable security. He informs me that this is the general feeling amongst the bankers in Winnipeg, but that they are unfavourable to the registration of aliens.
I have your letter inquiring as to the advisability of allowing banks to loan to farmers on their chattels. I have always been an advocate of this and know that in the Western States, it has worked out to the advantage of the small farmer in many cases.
If we were permitted to take security on the stock, we would certainly do more of this class of business.
The power to take security on live-stock would be distinctly useful. We certainly would lend more freely with this protection than without it. The chief difficulty which we encounter in dealing with farmers is in the matter of security. Endorsers are usually not available, and we are debarred from accepting the only collateral which a farmer has to give.
I think it would be an assistance to the farmers, particularly in the prairie section, if banks could get a lien on cattle and other live stock at the time an advance is made. My replies to your questions are as follows:
1. I think such legislation would facilitate and lead to increased advances by our bank to the stock-raising community and consequently, it would tend to increase production.
Replying to question No. 1, in your favour of the 24th ultimo, while I am inclined to the belief that, speaking generally, legislation authorizing the banks to take as security for advances to farmers or cattle raisers, liens on cattle and other live stock, might possibly facilitate lending to the stock-raising community, if it is found necessary, as you seem to think it would be, that any lien taken as security should be registered, I am of the opinion that any good which might be done by having this power would be offset to a very considerable extent by the trouble and expense of registering the said liens. You ask the question whether such legislation would lead to increased advances by this bank to the stockraising community. I am not prepared to say that it would lead to increased advances. In so far as this bank is concerned, our custom has been to lend to a farmer where his position has been satisfactory, without exacting security, excepting in the autumn sometimes, when he was able to put up warehouse receipts

for grain, but our lendings have been very largely on the general financial position of the man and his moral character.
Replying to the points you raise:
1. I think it would be advisable to give farmers the right to borrow against cattle and sheep by a pledge to the banks without registration. The question of animals being covered by previous chattel mortgages will have to be provided for. [DOT]
1. The suggested Legislation would doubtless lead to increased advances by this bank to the stock-raising community, and it should tend to increase production. It would probably not benefit the homesteader or the small farmer to the extent 'that might be expected. Advances to farmers of this class, whether with or without security, must always continue to be a moral risk. The questions of feed,' housing, and the borrower's reliability would always have to be considered.
1. Our long established policy throughout Canada is to lend to the farming community who apply to us in all cases where they are entitled to credit. It does seem to me, however, that the proposed legislation would facilitate and lead to increased advances by the banks and should therefore tend to increased agricultural production.
1. Legislation such as is under consideration would in all probability lead to increased advances by this bank and would tend to increased production of live stock.
1. In our opinion, the suggested legislation provides a simple and direct method for security on live stock and should tend to facilitate bank advances.
It will thus be seen that about half the chartered banks take a position favourable to this measure. Now, I give a few extracts from letters received from banks whose managers believe that the legislation will not accomplish what we have in view.

I do not doubt the accuracy of the letters, but we would like to have the names. Particularly, I would ask the minister if he could give us the opinion of two prominent bankers-say, the president of the Canadian Bank of Commerce for one, because that bank has so many agencies in the West, and of Sir Frederick Williams-Taylor, general manager of the Bank of Montreal, for another. Letters given without names have not the same effect as those that are signed. It is very important to have the names of the gentlemen who have written their opinions on this subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On general principles I entirely agree with my hon. friend as to this point. I would much rather put on Hansard the complete letters. But I do not feel at liberty to do so. So far as the

hon. gentleman himself is concerned, I shall take the opportunity of acquainting him with the views of the gentlemen to whom he has referred. I hope that will meet his wishes.
It is because some banks have so many branches in the West that I suggest that the names should be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am willing to put the extracts on Hansard, but if my hon. friend objects to my withholding the names I shall refrain from reading the extracts. I desire that this Bill shall be considered by the House absolutely on its merits, and my only object in giving these extracts is that the House may see that there are two points of view on the subject. As I stated when the resolution was under consideration, when we come to consider the matter in committee I want to have a very full discussion, so that we may reach a proper conclusion.
Are these letters from the managers, from the officials at the head offices, or from the officials in charge of offices in the western provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The replies are from managers of head offices; in some cases the views of their western managers are given. I may say, generally speaking, that the western managers are in favour of this legislation. I shall read two or three extracts from letters expressing the negative view:
I am satisfied, and absolutely so, that should you decide to amend the Bank Act, authorizing the banks to take liens upon cattle and certain other live stock, it would not result in our assisting the stock-raising community any more generously than we are doing at present.
Here is another:
I cannot see that the proposed legislation would be likely to make any appreciable increase in our advances to the stock-raising community.
Another one:
Re amendment to the Bank Act authorizing banks to take as security for advances to farmers' liens upon cattle and certain other live stock, I do not think such legislation would facilitate or lead to any increase in advances by banks to stock-raisers.
Here is another opinion:
I do not think that legislation giving the bank a lien upon the cattle is desirable, or would tend to increase advances for stockraising purposes.
Another bank says:
Such legislation as you mention would not lead to increased loans by this bank. We are

always ready to encourage and assist, by making liberal advances, those farmers desirous of increasing the production of live stock.
After receiving those letters, and after I had drafted the Bill which I have introduced to the House, I received a telegram, dated January 21, 1916, from the president and the secretary-treasurer of the United Farmers of Alberta. As this telegram, which has been published, is not confidential, I am quite sure that there can be no objection to placing it upon our records. It is as follows:
Calgary, Alta., Jan. 21, 1916. Sir Thomas White,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa.
Following resolution moved by Dunham, seconded by Trego, both vice-presidents, and passed unanimously:
Whereas, many farmers have large quantities of feed stuffs available but are not able to make profitable use of these because they cannot borrow money from the banks to buy horses, cows, cattle, sheep, and hogs, even if they are prepared to give security to the banks; and whereas, the Bank Act does not permit the banks to lend money to small farmers for such purposes and to take security over the live stock; resolved, that we, the United Farmers of Alberta, in convention assembled, request the Dominion Government at the present session of Parliament to amend the Bank Act so that small farmers may have the privilege of borrowing at long dates from the banks on the security of live stock. Note: This to apply to live stock held unencumbered or purchased after the amendment is passed because it is not suggested that securities already given over live stock should be interfered with.
H. Wood, President,
P. P. Woodbridge, Sec.-Treas., United Farmers of Alberta.
When this matter was under discussion the other day, the question was raised as to whether there had been any advantage to the western farmers from the legislation under which the banks were permitted to make advances upon the security of grain. As the statement was made that members were not aware of -any such advances having been made, I have taken the trouble to get for the information of the House an article which was referred to by one hon. gentleman from the Grain Growers Guide of Wednesday, February 2, 1916. With the consent of the House, I should like to put this also upon Hansard:
Borrowing on Grain.
Several times in these colums we have asked for information from our readers to show whether or not the banks were loaning money to farmers on the security of the threshed grain on their farms. Up till two weeks ago we were unable to get a report from any farmer who had succeeded in making such loans. Since that time, however, we have received a considerable number of reports showing that the banks are loaning money to farmers on the security of their grain in accordance with the amendment to the Bank Act, section 88, made three years ago. We find that many of the banks doing business with the farmers [DOT] in the West are loaning to the farmers on this security, and that some of the banks in particular are loaning quite extensively. Undoubtedly quite a number of the loans made on the security of the grain would have been made on the general standing of the farmer without such security, but our information is to the effect that a large number of farmers who would not have been able to borrow money from the banks under ordinary circumstances, have been able to do so by giving their threshed grain as security. This fact indicates that the amendment to the Bank Act was a benefit to the farmers of the West. It would seem, therefore, that any farmer who has a quantity of grain safely stored on his farm and insured, should be able to borrow a reasonable amount from his nearest bank. No doubt there is more money being borrowed on this security during the present year than ever before, because of the immense crop and the impossibility of putting it on the market as rapidly as has been done in years past. On account of the shortage of ships to take the wheat away from the eastern seaboard the wheat has been backed up clear to the Rocky mountains. Practically all storage capacity has been filled or will be filled by the amount of wheat now moving eastward. We receive letters regularly from farmers who tell us that they have several thousand bushels of wheat but have up to date not been able to market any of it because the elevators are full, the car-order book has several hundred names on it, and there are very few cars being received at their shipping points. In view of these facts the banks have a great opportunity this year for helping out the farmers by making advances on their grain on the farm until such time as it can be placed on the market.
In answer to question 3 in the letter which I addressed to the banks, the banks all assure me that there will be abundance of bank accommodation to meet the industrial and agricultural needs of the community during the coming year. A good deal of criticism has been directed against the banks for failing to lend where, in the opinion of hon. members, loans should have been made. It is to be borne in mind that the lending of money is a transaction that requires a good deal of judgment and care. The banks have a dual relationship; 'they have a relationship towards the depositing public, and they have a relationship towards the borrowing public. They are trustees of the funds of their shareholders, and of the funds entrusted to them by their depositors. The safe investment of money is, therefore, a prime consideration of the bankers. As they can only make money by lending their money at higher rates than those at which they borrow it, it would seem to be their interest to lend wherever good security can be obtained,

and upon personal credit if personal credit is such as appeals to them. My own view is that this legislation will be distinctly helpful in the way of obtaining advances to the western and other farmers upon the security of their livestock. I have no doubt, however, that the element of personal standing and credit will be of large, if not determining, weight with the banker in considering the question of whether or not advances should be made. I know that all members of the House have but one idea with regard to this matter, and that is to adopt legislation that will facilitate the extension of credit along safe and sound lines to our great agricultural community. I know that the banks are very desirous of in every way possible assisting to increase production, especially during the period of the war. Only a few weeks ago I wrote the banks a letter, which unfortunately I have not with me, in which I emphasized the importance of the banks, during the war, extending credits wherever they could safely do so in order to promote and encourage production. The great question in Canada to-day is that of increasing our production in order to meet the wastage of the war and to keep ourselves strong for the struggle which lies before us. I pointed out in this letter to the banks that the great danger in a time like this as that of inflation, the encouragement of speculation in either securities or commodities. I stated that I was aware that the banks were fully seized of the importance of that aspect of the matter. But I stated further that to make advances for the purpose of increasing production was wise policy, not only from the national standpoint, by its influence and effect in increasing production, but in making for the prosperity of the whole community, in which the banks, of course, are as much interested as any other class in the community. I am very glad to say that the banks have acted upon my request and are taking steps and will take steps to do their utmost to facilitate production, and especially agricultural production, during the coming year.

Did any of the banks
except the one referred to say that they did not think it would be wise to register the liens?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is only one that deals with the matter. My view would be that the banks would probably prefer that the lien should not be registered. But that raises the very important. question of

notice to creditors and purchasers for valuable consideration without notice. I explained to the House when the resolution was under consideration that I have simply placed the banks in the same position as any individual or company that has power to loan upon chattel mortgage in a province, and such chattel mortgage shall then become subject to the laws of that province as to registration and legal consequences.

I should like some
explanation in reference to the differences in the laws of different provinces as to the requirements of affidavits amd so on. Is it understood that in such particulars the security taken is to be subject to the laws of the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
ganized for the purpose of issuing short credits, for the purpose of loaning on the standing of the men who apply for ' loans and not on security. The farmer, as a rule, wants a longer credit, and it seems to me that a better way to get at this would be to have rural banks. If you have rural [DOT]banks they would give longer credits than the chartered banks, and they would not be on the same footing as an ordinary bank for the reason that, I imagine, people would be a little more careful about put-ing call deposits into a bank whose known purpose was to lend out money on long dates. They would be more unlikely to put deposits into banks of that kind. But I think that something should be done by the Minister of Finance in the way of helping these banks by perhaps giving them some of the assistance which is now given to our present banking system.
It is true that my hon. friend proposes to tax the banks somewhat in his new taxation Bill, but after all that is only a trifle to the banks.. In the first place, we give the banks, not an absolute, but a practical monopoly of all deposits in the Dominion of Canada. In addition, we give them the privilege of issuing an amount of paper money equal to their paid-up capital and we require them to make a deposit in gold with the Government to the extent of five per cent of the amount of that issue. I understand that the Government allow them three per 'cent on that deposit. So that the taxation imposed on the banks is only a trifle compared with what we give them. We give them with one hand a great, big bonus, a monopoly of the deposits of the country, the right to issue money free of cost, except the cost of printing the bills, and then we take back a small amount in taxation. The banks are in a different position from that of any other financial institution in the country. Other financial institutions do not get the advantages that the banks get and it occurs to me that something should be done along the line of withdrawing some of the advantages that we give to the banks under our present banking system, advantages that no other country on the face of the earth gives to its banks-bonuses and privileges such as banks in no other country get. It seems to me that something should be done in the way of withdrawing a portion of these priv-iliges, not to hurt the banks in any way, not to cripple them, and that we should establish a system of rural banks that would be of some real advantage to the farmer. I am sure that every man in this House who has ever been engaged in farming will un-

derstand that, if a farmer borrows money for the purpose of securing stock, he has to have that money for a considerable length of time in order to enable him to grow the stock, market it, get his money back with a profit and be in a position to pay off the debt. No three or six months' note will cover that.
It depends on what kind of live stock he is dealing with.

I understand that quite readily. In the case of hogs and sheep, even a moderate credit would cover it, but in most cases I think that farmers would want to go in for cattle as well as sheep and hogs. As far as sheep and hogs are concerned, my hon. friend from North Ox-for (Mr. Nesbitt) is quite right, but with respect to the bulk of the money that would be needed from the banks, there would require to be longer term credits. Long term credits cannot very well be got under our present system and they can be very much more easily got under a system of rural banks whose business it would be to grant longer credits and who would make arrangements for that purpose.
I do not want to be understood as opposing this proposal because it may be all right and it may be a help in some ways, but it does not seem to me that we are going far enough or that we are getting at the root of the trouble. There is a big agitation all through the west in favour of rural banks, or better still, farmers' credits, and a system of this kind should be worked out. While this may be a step in thp right direction, it does not seem to me that it goes far enough to accomplish very much.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to see the stand that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has taken on the question of the amendment of the Bank Act. In the province of Alberta, from which an application has come through the United Farmers, there is a strong agitation against the course which has been pursued by the banks during the last three or four years. My own impression in regard to the legislation which was put through two years ago in connection with liens on grain is, that it has not been of very material advantage. In conversation with one or two bank managers, I have been informed that they prefer to advance money to the farmer on the security of his own note, endorsed if possible. The unfortunate part of it is that they almost entirely insist on obtain-

ing an endorsement in connection with any loans made to the farmer. But, in consequence of this amendment, and judging from the extracts which the Minister of Finance has read, I would be inclined to think that banks would be more likely to advance money on security of this nature. As the minister has said, this legislation is largely for the benefit of Western Canada, and as the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) has pointed out, it is practically essential that the people should know what banks favour legislation of this character. In Western Canada there are only about six banks which do an active business in their branches. These six banks, excluding possibly the Bank of Montreal, are doing an extensive business with the small commercial interests and farmers. If we had the assurance that the Bank of Commerce, the Imperial Bank, the Union Bank, the Merchants Bank, and the Royal Bank were in favour of this legislation and were prepared to loan money to farmers .on security of this character, the farmer would be greatly reassured, for these banks practically control the business of the farmer and the small merchant in the West. There has been a great deal of dissatisfaction, perhaps not so much among the farmers as among the mercantile interests and others, at the action taken by the banks during the past year. Once a loan becomes past due, the banks, under the present Bank Act, are allowed to take the security, and on account of the pressure which they can bring to bear on the debtor they exact the utmost security. I know, personally, of instances where men have had to give security up to thirty or forty thousand dollars for a loan of $1,000 or $1,500; they were morally forced to give this security; they knew that if they refused the banks would call in the loan. This is a very arbitrary method for the banks to adopt, and I should like to see the Bank Act amended so that the banks would not have this tremendous power in their hands. We are giving them great privileges, and I think the Act should be so amended that the banks would not have the power of life and death, commercially speaking, placed in their hands. I agree with the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) that the minister does not go far enough in his amendments.

I notice that section 1 proposes to repeal the clause in the Act of last year which limited to August 1,
1915, the banks' powers in the matter of taking security for money advanced for seed grain. The effect of this amendment, I take it, will be to remove that restriction, and render it possible for a bank to take security on money which it may have advanced after that date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This simply removes the limitation as to time, and will enable the banks to do, during this year and next, what last year's Act enabled them to do last year.

Heretofore the policy in Canada has been along the lines of refusing to make amendments to the Bank Act, except under exceptional circumstances. We have had a lot of inroads upon that theory within the last few years; we have had the legislation of 1914, and of 1915, and now we have the legislation before us, creating new conditions under which banks can do business. Our friends from the West who have spoken on this Bill seem to think that it will mean that money will be lent more freely. I do not believe that it will have any such effect at all. My experience and practice of something over twenty years has been that in the East live stock is about the poorest security you can give for a loan, whether it is given by bill of sale or chattel mortgage. To my mind, therefore, the advantage will be more fancied than real. The Finance Minister has given us some correspondence which indicates a difference of opinion among banking people as to the usefulness of legislation of this character. As the minister, is amending the Act, I think he might as well go a little further and provide that a bank may loan money on -any personal property whatever; and not on live stock, merely, which is the most perishable kind of security, being animate life which may expire at any time, and which ' is subject to disease and pests which	may at any time wipe the
security out. This legislation practically says that the banks may loan money upon live stock in the West, but not in the East, and I do not think that that is wise. Though the banks would have power in any portion of the East to loan money on this security, just the same as is in the West, T think that any man in the East who, under this legislation, will be able to borrow from a bank on live stock security will need to have a very special case. If we are going to enter upon a new era in regard to banking conditions in this

.532
country, and 'allow the banks to take a bill of sale or chattel mortgage upon live stock, I think we might as well avoid the discrimination that is sure to exist under this legislation by going further and allowing the banks to loan money upon personal property generally. Why should we allow a man who may be interested in the live stock interest to borrow money from a bank upon the security of live stock, and exclude another man from borrowing money whose security consisted of personal property? A wealthy man who has money in bank stocks or bonds can go to the banks and raise money, but the poor main who has personal property and cannot get an endorser cannot get money from the bank on the security of his personal security, although the security may be just as good. If we are to enter upon a new policy, my suggestion is that instead of using the limited phraseology:
The bank may lend money to farmers and those engaged in stock-raising upon the security of their live stock.
We say, " The bank may lend money upon personal property." The wording of the Bill at present limits the conditions considerably. The word "farmers" is a word of special significance. For instance, a man not actually engaged in the tilling of the soil may he interested or engaged in the development of live stock; and if he is pressed by unfortunate conditions, which are liable to occur at any time, and seeks to borrow money from the banks, he will be unable to get it, for technically he would not be a farmer. Why does the minister not go the whole length and allow banks to lend money upon personal property? Let him cut out entirely ' the words "to farmers and those engaged in stock raising." If the minister is going to provide for future conditions, I urge him to empower the banks to loan money upon personal property generally; in that way he would avoid discrimination, he would avoid class legislation. This would not be compelling the banks to lend; under this legislation the banks are not compelled do lend a five cent piece more, they aire allowed to take a certain kind of security. The question is to get the banks to lend money at all. The fact that you remove a technical objection in order to enable the banks to give a loan, is not going to make them more willing to lend money if the borrower is not satisfactory. A bank will be all the more ready to lend money when the borrower has

personal property of any kind and is a man of integrity in the community, and there will not be the same difficulties if you tie the matter up, as is done in this Bill.
As a matter of strict law, it might be argued whether or not the - phraseology of section 12 is not such that the power to lend money is given to the bank only when the loan is upon the security of livestock alone. The bank may say: well, we might lend that money to you, but we want to get an endorser. As this clause is enabling legislation, it might be urged that a loan on the security of livestock alone would render illegal the taking of an endorsement as well. I have heard in regard to promissory notes arguments which, although they did not seem to have as much in them as my argument, have been sustained by the courts. All these difficulties would be done away with if my hon. friend would make it clear that the endorsation could accompany the loan and not invalidate it. In all our eastern provinces, outside of the question of lending money on stock in warehouses, the proposed provisions in this Bill are not likely to be taken advantage of to a great extent. In the eastern provinces, the banks require an endorser in the first instance, but there is no reason why, on account of the financial restrictions owing to the wiar, the East will mot be equally interested in this Bill and in the operation of its provisions. Therefore, I am urging upon the minister, while he is dealing with the amendment of the Bank Act at this juncture, to permit a loan to be made on personal property and good security by a bill of sale or chattel mortgage, the same as may be done by a private investor. There are some other matters which I intend to bring up when we go into committee on this Bill. In his speech the other day the Minister of Finance said :
It is probable that in the straitened financial conditions which may prevail for some years forward the question of capital for the development of agriculture may be of paramount importance, and it is our intention to inquire carefully during the coming recess into this most important subject,, with a view, if desirable in the public interest, to supplrminting by federal aid existing facilities in this connection. Particularly will the question of establishment of a system whereby loans at reasonable rates repayable on the amortization principle engage the attention of the Government.
We therefore enter upon the fringe of what may come to be wide and important legislation in this matter. The avenue along which my hon. friend will enter in regard

to agricultural questions is one which will lead him into other lines where the development of other kinds of industries will make claims upon him with equal force. Take for instance the fish industry, where people have gone from the use of old-fashioned sail boats to motor boats which have now become essential to the pursuit of their business. The request by men engaged in that industry, that the aid given along one line should also be extended to them seem to me to involve a proposition which the minister would be bound to consider as being of equal importance. And so it will be argued in regard to other lines of business. I gather from what the minister said the other day, from the discussion that has taken place here, and from the provisions of this Bill, that we nave now reached that stage in banking legislation where we are opening the door to the banks to take security in wider forms than ever before. The general conditions throughout the country has brought that about. The minister, therefore, might as well strip the whole legislation of the limitations which he is putting in this Bill; he might as well prevent what will be urged as class legislation, by simply providing that the banks may lend money on personal property and take security therefor by bills of sale, or chattel mortgages, as other investors may do.

This question is one which affects me as' an Ontario farmer who is deeply interested in the welfare of the western farmer. I take it that this Bill has been introduced because representations have been made to the Minister of Finance that there was a demand for these changes. The farmers of the West have been giving these matters very serious consideration, and which has been increased by the demand for mixed farming, and by the fatet that between forty and fifty thousand cattle have been shipped out of the Northwest to the United . States markets. That fact to a certain extent should be deplored, because many of these cattle were in -an unfinished -state, and many of them were females which were needed badly in our western provinces. Two parties are deeply interested in this question: the man who wants to sell his stock and the man who wants to buy. The man who wiants to sell needs to raise money in some shape or form -and one of the easiest forms in which he can raise it is by disposing of his cattle. He can easily find a neighbour who wants to buy, but unfortunately that neighbour, although he may have the
feed, has not the money to pay for the cattle. The one has the feed but not the cattle; the other has the cattle but not the feed. Under this Bill the man who may be forced to sell for want of money should be able -to raise the money- easily. It is true that the banks have not been -as popular with the farmers in years gone by as they might have been, but to my mind, a big change has come over the feelings of bankers during the last four or five years, and they are beginning to realize the fact that farmers are, to a very large extent, business men, and that if they are helped, it will in turn help the business prosperity of this country.
This matter, perhaps, has taken more pronounced form from the fact that in some states of the Union subsidiary companies have been formed which lend money to the farmers and become bondsmen, as it were, to the hanks; or the banks lend the money and these companies become sureties for the payment. But. while I think that great good can be accomplished by these companies, I am a little afraid of their operation. They are generally backed by the packers of the large cities, and taking these men generally they are more deeply interested in speculative prices than -anything elsfe-to a certain extent they live upon speculative prices.
I take it to be scarcely possible that the western farmers would be opposed to the propositions of the Minister of Finance, for those propositions will be to their interest. It is true -that many of them have been able to procure money upon their own notes in the past, but many others have not been able to do so. If the conditions can be made more liberal in the days to come than they have been in the past, so much the better for them. It has been said that the trouble was with short credits. I agree with that statement. I think that was one of the mistakes the banks made. The money was often loaned for three months, and at the end of that -time, on account of trade conditions, they wanted the money back. I need scarcely say the farmer could not finish the cattle in three months, and he needed the money for the longer period. If I understand the temper and feeling of the bank managers to-day,- they favour making credits longer than three months. If the animals have to be sold at the end of three* months, the profits are so small, that nothing accrues to the feeders. The time should be extended so that the cattle ^may go out in a finished state. If this is done, instead of these animals going to

the markets to the south of us, the chances are that many of them may drift to our eastern provinces._ While it may be said that this would not do the consumer any good, I believe that the effect would be to so regulate prices in the eastern provinces that the consumer would be better off in the end, while the producer in the West would be none the worse. I cannot take any -other view of this Bill than that it will help the western farmer, and in helping the western farmer it will be just as sure to do good to the farmer in the East.

I regret that this Bill has been drafted on narrow lines. We have the fishermen of the Maritime Provinces who aTe equally entitled to consideration with the farmers of the West. From time to time, the fishermen are obliged to depend upon advances for the purpose of carrying on their operations, and I regret that this Bill does not contain a provision whereby they could more readily obtain.the credits which will assist them in carrying on their industry successfully. This Act, so far as I apprehend its meaning, will not make it any easier for our people in Nova Scotia, nor for the people elsewhere in Canada, to obtain loans. In Nova Scotia, the bank managers insist on having one endorser, if not more, upon every note that is sought to be discounted. If the Finance Minister would put a clause in this Bill to compel the bank managers to advance money upon the security of personal property, I think some good would be accomplished. But, even if this Act is passed, and even if it should be made applicable to all classes of personal property, our farmers and fishermen would find it just as difficult to obtain credit in the bank as they have found it before.
I have an observation to make with regard to the drafting of the second section of the Act. That section is as follows:
2. Section eighty-eight of the Bank Act is further amended by adding thereto the following subsections:
12. The bank may lend money to farmers and those engaged in stock raising upon the security of their live stock. " Live stock," for the purposes of this subsection and of subsections thirteen to sixteen, both inclusive, means horses and their progeny, bulls and cows and their progeny, swine and sheep.
I take it that this section means that if a man has a stallion and obtains a loan on the value of the animal the security extends equally to the animal's progeny. But the common law is that the progeny follows the dam. Therefore, if a man owned a mare upon the security of which money

had been advanced, the bill of sale applies to the colt as well, whereas according to this section of the Act, if it has any meaning at all, that principle will be reversed. Under this proposed law a bill of sale given upon a male animal would apply to the progeny, while a bill of sale upon a female animal, owned perhaps, by a wholly different person, would equally apply to the progeny. Perhaps I do not understand the meaning of the section, but it seems to me that some correction ought to be made so that it may not lead to confusion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend really serious? I assume he is. If he is, may I explain to him that the word " cattle ' is standard, it is generic, and it is absolutely necessary to have the wording as it is in order to cover the male animal, the female and the calf.

What is the meaning
of it? The system in many parts- of the country is that a stallion is used to get colts in various parts of a district on dams in different ownership. The owner of the dam, apparently, will not participate in the loan. [DOT] Does the Bill mean that the colt, when horn, is mortgaged to the owner of the stallion, or to the owner of the dam?

I would like an explanation on one point-as to what the rights of the banks are to be under this bill of sale. I am not familiar with the laws relating to chattel mortgages in prov-. inces other than Nova Scotia. I have found that our laws of that kind generally closely resemble those of Ontario. No doubt, as has been suggested by an hon. friend near me, Ontario copies Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia if a man gives as security for payment of a note, a bill of sale upon certain property, the person who holds the bill of sale may take possession of that property if default is made by the borrower. It is not a settled point in our province whether the man who takes a horse, for instance, under a bill of sale, is obliged to sell the animal, or whether he may keep it in satisfaction of his claim. The minister does not -catch what I say; if he does not think it worth his while listening, I shall direct my observations to the Chair.

I merely wish to interject the remark that I was discussing for a moment with the minister exactly the point that was -being raised. I heard every

word the hour, member said, and I have no doubt the minister did also.

If the minister says he did, I .am perfectly satisfied. For my own part I have found it difficult to listen to two persons at the same time, and to know what both are saying. I was saying that in Nova Scotia if .a man borrows $50 and gives security on a horse worth $200, in case of default being made it is quite competent for the person, or the bans holding the bill of sale to take absolute possession of the horse. Unless the person defaulting gets a decree from the court directing the sale of the animal and accounting for the difference between the proceeds and the amount of the claim, there is no provision in our Act giving the owner of the horse any remedy. Subsection 16 of section 88 of the Bank Act reads:
A security agreement in form H may be enforced by civil action in any court of competent jurisdiction.
There are a great many kinds of action; what kind of action should be taken under this provision? Is the bank obliged to obtain a decree of the court vesting the property in the bank, or is it the duty of the court to ascertain the value of the property and to decide how much shall go to the bank and .how. much shall be returned to the borrower? When we create a new law, the machinery should be made as definite as possible, so that the court will be left as little as possible to settle. I imagine that if a bank came into court under this subsection, it would be the duty of the court to decide the value of the property, perhaps direct the sale of it, and determine the amount to be paid the respective parties. But this would be a very expensive way for the farmer to find out how much was coming to him. The Act merely says that the owner of the property can assign it to the bank. At common law there must be an absolute assignment to give title. No absolute assignment is provided for here; an assignment which is not absolute merely gives a lien. Perhaps the insertion of the word "absolute" would overcome that difficulty. I make these observations merely to call the minister's attention to the fact that, so far as I can gather, no machinery is provided by this Act for determining what shall happen if there is default on the part of the person who gives property as security. The minister will see that some of us do not
understand the machinery that is provided for the ordinary operation of this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry that my hon. friend ~ should have thought that I was guilty of some discourtesy to him. I assure him that I was endeavouring to listen to what he said; he will realize that a minister is subject to more or less interruption from time to time, and I hope he will accept the explanation.
My hon. friend inquired as to the chattel mortgage legislation of Ontario. It is some years since I have been familiar with it, but I may say that in many respects it is similar to that of Nova Scotia. Under the English system, as my hon. friend knows, a mortgage vests the property in the mortgagee, and the property so vested- personal property in this case-may remain in the possession of the mortgagor until default. Upon default the mortgagee, under the terms of the mortgage, is entitled to pursue his remedies. There is usually a covenant in a chattel mortgage-I am speaking now of Ontario chattel mortgages -in which the mortgagor promises that he will pay the amount advanced. It is, therefore, open to the mortgagee to sue upon the covenant or to enforce his security through the courts, as he might in the case of a land mortgage if there were not some agreement or covenant to the contrary. *There is also in the Ontario chattel mortgage a power of sale which enables the mortgagee, upon giving the notice stipulated, to sell in accordance with the terms of the mortgage. Any surplus that he may have upon realization of the chattels and after payment to himself of the amount advanced, with interest and all charges, would, of course, belong to the mortgagor.
My hon. friend has called attention to Form II of the schedule. He will observe that in section 2 there is the following provision:
The hank may lend money to farmers and those engaged In stock-raising on the security of their live stock.
Then there is a definition of live stock:
The security agreement may be made in the form of a bill of sale or chattel mortgage, or, in any province where no provision exists in the laws of the province for the filing or other registration of bills of sale or chattel mortgages, then in the form H in the schedule .to this Act or in a form to like effect.
The intention of the legislation is that the bank may take a chattel mortgage in provinces where there is provision for the *registration of chattel mortgages. Usually, under the terms of such legislation, there

is a requirement of an affidavit of bona fides and provision for registration within a certain number of days. I think five days in the province of Ontario. The security agreement is intended to be used in provinces where the chattel mortgage is either not recognized by legislation or where no provision exists for such registration. I may call my hon. friend's attention to the last section in form H, which I think he has overlooked:
This security is given under the provisions at subsections twelve and thirteen of section eighty-eight of the Bank Act, and is subject to the provisions of the said Act.
The Bank Act itself provides for !the method of realization of the security. What we had in mind in providing that the security agreement in form H might be enforced by the court, was that machinery might be provided for its realization as the court might direct in cases in which it might not be expedient 'to realize under the provisions of the Bank Act mentioned. That, in general terms, is what we had in view. Before the matter comes up in committee I should be very glad to give attention to the point brought up by my hon. friend, and shall be glad to have the benefit of his views in committee.
The hon. member for Pictou stated that we were making a departure, and that is true. The Bank Act, for many years, in fact ever since it was first enacted, has had in view that banks should make short date loans. The idea of quick
5 p.m. assets has always been present to legislators in considering legislation affecting banks. The reason is, of course, obvious. Bankers borrow from the public, and they borrow a large portion of their funds repayable on terms by which they may be asked to repay upon demand. Other deposits which they receive are upon notice. It is therefore of great importance to the banks that their assets should be of a quickly realizable character. That is to say, that their bills should be payable at short dates so that they may have money coming in from time to time which will enable them to meet their liabilities. Then in order to get the maximum of advantage to the community from the use of the bank capital, it is advisable that loans should be made for short date periods rather than that this capital should be tied up for long periods, because a bank will frequently be able to serve twenty customer's requiring, let us say, *$50,000, each representing a total of a million dollars, with much less than a million dollars of bank capital, b.e-

causd all the customers will not require the money at the same time. While that has been the policy of the banks and of all legislators in the past, my hon. friend, I know, recognizes that conditions are continually changing; and sometimes I think we fail to do justice to important sections of the community by reason of our failure to realize that conditions are changing, that new conditions are arising which have to be met by legislation. That is what has occurred in the West. Conditions in the West are different from conditions in the East. In the East the banks loan to farmers and others usually upon notes for which they have obtained endorsers. In the West it is very difficult to obtain satisfactory endorsers; and the result is that where the borrower is a man of good character and likely to succeed, where the moral risk, as they say, is good, then the bank has to face the question: Shall we make this loan? The bank might hesitate to make the loan if the borrower had not security; but, as has been pointed out, if he had the live stock security to pledge and if his credit was good, that is to say if the moral risk was looked upon as good, I think the loan would often be made where otherwise it would not be made. I think that is a justification for this legislation. In the case of sheep and hogs, I think the short term loan would be satisfactory; but in the case of cattle where it takes a couple of years or more to rear the animals to maturity, I think this legislation will be very useful. In the United States it is said to have been of supreme value to the stock raising industry, and over there the industry has been developed upon a large scale, with great benefit to the farming community, by reason of the facilities which are afforded under the banking legislation of the northwestern states whereby the banks are .permitted to lend upon chattel mortgage security. My hon. friend from Pictou has said: Why not go further and allow the banks to loan upon all personal property? Well'l, there is something to be said for that view, although I think I could mention many objections. At present'the banks loan to wholesale dealers and merchants upon commodities of all kinds. That has been the law and that, in a sense, was class legislation. It was regarded as necessary in the common in-. terest of the community. This is in a sense class legislation, if it can be called class legislation where we are only endeavouring to put the farmer in the same posi-

tion that a certain class of the business community 'has been in before. In time it may well occur that other interests will feel the need of some amendment of the Bank Act and they may say they think there might be an amendment under which they might be permitted to pledge personal property of their production to the bank. Should such an occasion arise, I should deem it my duty to consider such an application, or any representation made on that behalf, upon their merits. Hon. gentlemen know that bonds and stocks are personal property, but they are not classified as chattels under the chattel mortgage legislation of several of the provinces. It is a common transaction for an individual, as well as brokers, to pledge and hypothecate bonds and stocks as security for advances from banks.
When this matter comes before the committee it is my hope and wish that the proposed legislation will be thoroughly canvassed, because it does involve a departure and if, in the opinion of the majority of the committee, it is deemed advisable that a time limit should be put upon this legislation, so that it may, in a sense, be experimental, that will be well worthy of consideration. I remember that when we were bringing in the legislation of last session as to seed grain advances by banks, and permitting them to take security for such advances, my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) suggested, either by way of question, or by direct statement, that as it was war time an experiment might well be made. I would be prepared to consider, if the committee thought it desirable, a time limit in order that we might have the benefit of the experiment.
I have read over carefully the discussions since 1890 in connection with the successive revisions of the Bank Act and it is astonishing how history repeats itself. The arguments put forward here to-day, and when the resolution was under consideration, are precisely the arguments, pro and con, that were put forward in the old days, and I think it will interest hon. members of the House when I say that Mr. Donald Smith, afterwards Lord Strathcona, who knew the West as well as any man in the early nineties, was very strongly in favour of legislation of this character. I desire to thank the House for the very interesting discussion we have had and for the information which I have derived from the debate.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time.
On motion of Sir Thomas White, the Bill was referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce.

Sir THOMAS ' WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 34, to authorize certain extensions of time to insurance -companies. He- said:
Mr. Speaker, I explained, when the House was in committee upon the resolution which preceded this Bill, that the intention of the legislation was to extend the time in which insurance companies might apply for licenses under the provisions of the Insurance Act of 1910. There are outstanding a number of company charters which would terminate this year unless they have organized and put themselves in the position to comply with the requirements of the Insurance Act. On account of the conditions which have prevailed since the outbreak of the war, it has not been possible for these companies to organize, to get their stock subscribed so as to be in a position to obtain licenses under the Insurance Act. The purpose of the legislation is to enable them to do so without special application on their part to Parliament. The other day the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) asked me for the names of the companies whose charters were so outstanding, and which would expire, and I laid upon the table of the House a list of which I gave him a copy. I think there were some seven or eight of such companies. A precisely similar Act was passed by -the House last session.

Are these companies just being organized, or companies which have been organized, and which have to conform with some provision within >a required time?
Sir THOMAS WHI-TE: They are companies which were incorporated by Parliament, but my hon. friend knows that before they get a license under the Insurance Act they must have a certain amount of their capital subscribed and paid up. On account of the outbreak of the war and on account of the conditions which have prevailed since the war it has not been possible for these companies to get their stock subscribed as would have been the case had times remained normal. If a charter was about to lapse the ordinary course would

be for the company to make a new application by private Bill for an extension of the term. This is rather costly, and for the convenience of these companies' we have thought it advisable to bring in this Bill in the same terms as the Bill of last year, extending for one year the period in which they may comply with the provisions of the Insurance Act.

What is the policy of
the hon. Minister of Finance in regard to this matter? Does he think it a wise policy to continue extending the charter of a company that has been unable to comply with the terms of the Act? I understand we are leaving the whole matter in the dispretion of his department, and that any of these companies will be at liberty to apply to him, or his department, to get an extension. Are we to understand that these extensions are to be granted to any company without any investigation or any requirements on the part of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The policy has been not to lightly permit the renewal of charters, but I have not known of a case in which the Banking and Commerce Committee or the House have refused a private Bill for the extension of a charter when it has been shown to the satisfaction of the committee and the House that reasonable efforts have been made by the promoters of the company to capitalize it and to comply with the provisions of the Insurance Act. There is usually strong objection to a second renewal and that would obtain in this case were it not for war conditions. If it were not for war conditions I should not have introduced this Bill because if a company has been given an extension, and if it has failed to comply with the requirements of the Insurance Act, I think'it should be' called upon to show cause why it should be given a further extension.
