As this is probably the last item on which I can bring this subject up, I should like to ask the minister why fSir Thomas White.]
Inspector Heffemian of the Northwest Mounted Police was not given his ordinary promotion, and why two junior officers were put over his head, practically compelling him to resign? I do not ask the minister to reply now, but he might have this information for me when his estimates come up again.

I would point out that the Royal Northwest Mounted Police are not in my department, but in the Prime Minister's. I will direct his attention to the hon. gentleman's question.
Government of the Yukon Territory-salaries and expenses connected with the administration of the territory, $128,000.
What is the population of the Yukon? How are conditions there generally? We should economize in these times; what is the justification for all this expenditure?
I will ask the hon. member for the Yukon to answer that.

I am very
glad indeed to be able to give my hon. friend the information which he asks for. I might preface my remarks by saying that it is very much easier to economize in the older and more settled sections of Canada than in outlying territories such as the Yukon. The Yukon is a very large territory-about 200,-000 miles in extent; it is sparsely settled, and we have found it difficult to adjust the cost per annum to the variations of our population. Miners go out from the settled centres to outlying districts and prospect for gold and silver, copper, coal, petroleum, etc., and the Government gives them every possible assistance in carrying on this work, which we conceive' to be for the benefit not only of the Yukon but of the whole of Canada. We have also roads to build, trails to cut, steamship lines to subsidize. We have found it difficult to adjust our expenditure to a lower amount than we are asking for this year. I am sure that every dollar that was spent by the Government in the Yukon last year was spent well, and I believe that if the House passes this vote the country will be given full value for the money.

Does this include the cost
of administration of justice in the Yukon?

I think there is a
separate vote for the administration of justice. As the item explains, there is a grant to Local Council for maintenance and re-

pairs of roads. Our population, according to the census of 1911, was 9,000. I do not think it has increased since that time.
How much has it decreased?

The last official
figures I have are the census figures for 1911, when the population was 9,000. We are producing between four and a half and five million dollars worth of gold every year.

By the use of gold
dredges?

About 80 per cent of the gold is recovered by dredging. These gold dredges are huge machines, and it may be interesting to the House to learn that we have in the Yukon the largest gold dredges in the world.
Tell us about them.

They are driven by electricity created by the water-power of the Klondike river and conveyed. oveT wires to the seat of operation. They float in their own ponds .and work twenty-four hours a day. The gold is recovered by a system of washing the gravel and carrying it through a series of operations. The cost of operation is being gradually reduced year by year, and thereby the basis of our pay-streak is being widened annually. This refers particularly to the older settled portions of the Yukon and those districts within striking distance of Dawson City. The auriferous area of the Yukon is not confined to those particular districts; large areas of gold-bearing gravel still await the prospector and the hydraulic operator. The cost of transportation is very considerable, and the cost of operation in the past has been so great that only the richer portions of the gold-bearing gravel could be mined profitably. Year by year, however, as the industry is becoming standardized, so to speak, the operating costs are decreasing, and therefore the low-grade gravels are being worked from time to time. New districts are opening up, .and the future of the Yukon, I believe, was never better than it is at the present time.
We are successfully mining silver ores in the Yukomr-ores that go between two and three hundred dollars in silver per ton. We also have in the Yukon perhaps the largest antimony deposits in the world, certainly the largest on this continent ot on this side of China.
What is the location of them?

The antimony deposits are in the vicinity of the Wheaton district, which is between lake Bennett and Whitehorse, about twenty miles along the Whitehorse railway. They were examined during the past year by Dr. Cairnes, an eminent geologist in the employ of the Government, and reported upon by him.
I am not sure that the report is yet published, but if any hon. member is interested in antimony, he will find very interesting information in that report.
Are the antimony deposits being worked?

copper belt has already been published by Mr. McConnell, Deputy Minister of Mines. It is in the archives of the Mines branch, and I would commend that report to any one interested in copper.
There are huge areas of land in the Yukon that are capable of being developed as grazing lands, and some of our citizens are paying attention to that particular line of industry so that altogether the future of the Yukon is most bright and hopeful, and the last page of its history has not been written by any means. I feel sure that the committee, in passing this vote, will be doing credit to itself, and the money will be well expended, and will return from the Yukon like bread thrown on the waters.

Can my hon. friend tell me about the creek called Too-Much-Gold? A friend of mine was interested in it, but he told me that he had received nothing from his investment. He was carried away by the name.

The name is certainly an attractive one, but I am afraid that the hopes raised by the name were not justified. There is a creek in the Yukon known as Too-Much-Gold, and the tradition is that the Indians, who were living on that creek when the white prospectors went there, had named it Too-Much-Gold or some name similar to that, and the prospectors adopted the name. I do not think, however, that that creek has produced any gold to speak of.

I find the very large item of $90,000 for the administration of justice. For looking after 9,000 people in the Yukon, it is costing this country $443,000. Although my hon. friend the member for the Yukon (Mr. Thompson) has given the most optimistic view that could be given of that portion of the Dominion, the amount is a very large one per capita, especially if we take into account the fact that the population has been stationary, if not decreasing, during the past five years. It is larger than the provincial subsidy for some of the provinces. Now, it is a fair subject for consideration whether or not, in view of the fact that this territory adjoins British Columbia, the administration of provincial affairs under the British North America Act could not be transferred to British Columbia. It is a great anomaly that we should keep such a panoply of organized state in order to deal with 9,000 people. A friend who has made^ the calculation tells me that it amounts to $49 per 
capita. Conditions are changed from those-which existed when the Yukon was expected to have a very large population. Though we have a minimum of population, we have all the machinery of Government for a vastly greater number of people. It seems to me that in this year of economy our expenditure in that part of the Dominion is too great. The minister ought to devise some means to economize. The business of the East is being taxed enormously in order to carry on the war, and there ought to be some concessions by these 9,000 people of the Yukon. I would like to know what the argument is in support of this expenditure.

I quite realize the force of the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald); but I am sure he will bear me out when I say that while it is easy to cast a scheme of government for a given population, it is not so easy to adjust that scheme to a decreasing population. There is a certain fixed charge, as in any other organization, below which it is impossible to go. For instance, you must have a court in that part of Canada; we are entitled to it.
But the expenditure involved is very large.
I would draw the hon. member's attention to the fact that even the labouring man, who has no more skill than is required to handle a pick and shovel, gets four dollars a day and board.
All the year round?

While he works. He works at mining, dredging, hydraulicking, in the summer, and if he works in the winter he gets the same wage.
Mr. OI,TVER:	How many months does
the season cover?

The season is being
extended. One dredge is working this year all winter,' I believe, but I fancy that six months would be the average, perhaps a fairly high average. The work begins in the latter part of March and ends in October, as a rule. One company has been able to operate its dredges until the beginning of the New Year, and I believe is even operating one all winter. One of the difficulties we have been confronted with is to-adjust the cost of governing the territory to the decreasing population. But that is not a new problem in the governing of western countries. When the province of British Columbia was admitted into this

*confederation-I quote from memory and subject to correction-she had not more than 25,000 white people, yet she was given a representation of six members in this House.	'
We are not dealing with representation; we are not thinking of cutting down the representation of the Yukon.

I thank my hon. friend for that. My point is that in considering these new countries, you must not think that the last stage has been reached. A stampede may occur, and an influx of population, at any time.
What internal taxation have you there?

That is another point, and I am glad my hon. friend reminded me of it. We have in the Yukon what you have not in any other province of Canada, a direct tax of 2i per cent on our principal output, that of gold.
Every province'pays royalties.

As a provincial tax,
but no province returns a tax on its output to the federal treasury.

But we more than
give that back in the expenditure we make.

What is the amount
of revenue derived from that royalty?
I am not arguing that our revenue is sufficient-
Is there any local taxation?

We have the municipal taxes of Whitehorse and Dawson. Then, of course, we have liquor licenses, the proceeds of which are used for road building. Besides, a tax is charged for recording a claim and for the annual renewal of a claim.	'*
Has the hon. gentleman any idea what the returns to the Dominion treasury are for the recording and renewal of claims?
Last year the revenue was $210,000 for all sources. -
What is the reason for the decrease in population?

Mining populations are notorious for their migratory habits. Gold miners especially are attracted to new countries by prospects of discovery. We
lost quite a large number of our population some years ago to Alaska, which is also a gold-mining country, and the conditions in which are very similar to those in Yukon. Some of our people went there, and are there to-day. It is quite within the realm of probability that they will come to the Yukon again if some of* the new strikes which are now being exploited prove as good as we hope they will.
What is the revenue from the recording and renewal of claims?

Royalty on gold in round figures, $116,000; placer grants, $9,000; placer renewals, $40,000; placer relocations, $3,000; quartz grants, $975; gold dredging leases, $5,000; hydraulic leases, $5,000; mining fees, $6,000; payments in lieu of work, $1,000; land sales, and quartz acreage, $2,900; rentals, $7,000; timber dues, $11,000; suspense account, $1,000; total, $210,000.

How many schools and
colleges are there in the Yukon?

We in the Yukon are on the very outposts of Canada; we are a part of Canada, and we are keeping up our share in this Canadian civilization of ours. Our schools are excellent. We have in Dawson a school which is not called a normal school, or a high school, but which gives students work equivalent to that of the first year in the University of Toronto or McGill. We send pupils from Dawson to the University of Toronto and to McGill to take second year work. We are, therefore, doing our share in keeping up the standard of education which we believe to be in the best interests of all Canada.
You have no more people there than would be found in a fair-sized town in any of our eastern provinces.
There are not more people in the whole of Nova Scotia than there are to the city of Toronto. .
But the Dominion Government does not pay them $44 a head to live in Nova Scotia.

The province of Nova Scotia, from which I came, and of which I am proud, passed through the same series of events which the . Yukon territory is passing through to-day. It did not come suddenly into existence, with a population of half a million, with great industries,

great commerce and great educational institutions; it had to grow, as the Yukon is growing. The same is true of the other provinces of Canada; the western provinces had their periods of good fortune and of bad fortune.

A few years ago my
hon. friend brought a bag of wheat and submitted it to the House as an indication of the fertility of the soil in the Yukon. Will my hon. friend tell the committee whether wheat is still grown in the Yukon?
I am glad to inform my hon. friend that we are growing some wheat in the Yukon.
Do you grow enough for your own needs?
No, we grow practically no wheat, unless it be for experimental purposes.

You grow vegetables,
do you not?
Yes, excellent vegetables: potatoes, carrots, cabbage, beans, barley, and quite a large quantity of oats. Some of the farms are very creditable indeed.

You ought to grow a
Yukon minister.

I hope in time that the Yukon may be important enough to have a minister; I thank my hon. friend for the suggestion. It may be interesting to the House to know that the wheat that I brought from the Yukon on that occasion proved to be of a very virile type. I sent a sample of it to the seed specialist at the experimental farm, who planted 100 grains. Of these 100 grains, 100 per cent germinated, which shows the possibilities of the seed we can grow in that country.

When I was Postmaster General there was considerable quarrelling about the postal service in the Yukon. Has the quarrel with the railway company been settled, and is the service in good running order?

Yes, excellent. The
embargo has been removed, and we can get all the mail all the time, which was one of the slogans that we used in the Yukon. I would draw the attention of the hon. member for Pictou to the fact that for years we had to pay double rates on money orders; we paid 60 cents where the

other parts of Canada paid only 30. In this respect we are now on the same basis as the rest of Canada.
I think you use the post office for the forwarding of gold-dust.
Yes. ,
Do you pay a high rate?
No, the rate is the same as that on any other commodity. The gold is smelted and made into small bricks and sent out by mail.
Do you pay insurance?
I am not sure about that.
Have you a rural mail service in the Yukon?

No.
Mr.'MACDONALD: I desire that the hon. member for Yukon should not misapprehend the position I take with regard to this matter. I am delighted to know that he is so confident about the future of the Yukon country; nothing would give me greater pleasure than to look forward to the development of that portion of Canada. The point that I desire to raise is whether or not we are paying this year for the administration of the affairs of the' Yukon the same amount that we paid when the population was double what it is to-day. If it be true that we are paying for administering the affairs of 9,000 people what it cost when the population was 20,000 or 25,000, I should like to ask whether, in view of the pronouncements made by hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House as to the necessity for strictest economy in these times, some amendment could not be made by which a saving could be effected. I say this in all friendliness to my hon. friend's constituency. Before this vote is passed I think we should know what the Yukon is costing us to-day, and what it'cost us, say, in 1910. Is there any reason why there should be no retrenchment in the Yukon if there is retrenchment in every other part of Canada.
Perhaps the hon. minister will bring down a list of the officials who are employed in the Yukon.
I have a list of them.

I feel like being generous to my hon. friend and to the territory he has the honour to represent; I do not think we should be too rigid in our criticism of

the expenditures out there. But at the same time I think there is a certain necessity for retrenchment. In looking at the Auditor General's Report of last year, I find that the total customs revenue is $164,000, and this has cost us about $30,000 to collect. There are a number of officers obtaining large salaries and large living expenses in the employment of the Customs Department. Although the amount collected is small and the expense so large, I see that one man has been working overtime, and is allowed $403 for overtime work. It is just possible that some of these salaries might be reduced, and that we do not need so' many customs officers for the collection of so small an amount as $164,000. I- know that the Minister of Customs believes in a large staff; we have learned that since he became minister. But it seems to me that it is up to him to look into that matter and see if he cannot trim the Yukon salary list a little.

Would the hon. member for the Yukon tell us where the northern
terminus in the Alaskan territory of this new American railway will be? Will it have any appreciable effect on the condition of the people in the Yukon as regards transportation facilities? Have they started the construction of that road at both ends?

They have not begun construction at both ends, but they have begun construction at the tide water end. That will be at a point called Seward, in Alaska, 600 miles west of Skagway, the port at which we land for the Yukon. The internal terminus of the road is said to be Fairbanks, which is in the heart of the goldbearing district of Alaska. Fairbanks is about 700 miles from Dawson, and I do not expect that the road will very materially alter the transportation affairs of the Yukon territory.
Progress reported.
